title: Fungal/Lichen Museum Specimen Extraction, Amplification, and Sequencing
author: Stephen D Douglas Russell
materials: Much like DNA extraction for old specimens, PCR itself is fickle/temperamental. It can fail the first time you attempt it, and then work the second time with exactly the same template, PCR cocktail, and thermocycler parameters. For this, we believe replication of PCR up front is an important part of any protocol for museum specimens. Begin by preparing PCR reactions. Primers are ordered using the ONT-tagged primers and Master Mix protocol. We prepare all of our dual-index primer plates on an Opentrons OT2 liquid handling robot. For each herbarium specimen we give multiple PCR attempts. Typically one attempt with long reads (ITS1F-ITS4) and another attempt with short reads (ITS2 - gITS7-ITS4). Note on primers: The forward primers all have a single unique index per 96-well plate and the reverse primers all have a unique index for each of the 96 specimens specimen on the plate (a plate of reverse primers with 96 different indexes). This strategy allows us to extend the number of samples per library far beyond the ONT Nanopore barcoding kit of 96 samples, but does require you to order your own primer combinations. We have these premade for order in the main protocol above. Amplification from ENA extracts: Depending on how important the collections are and how high of success rates we want to see, the amount of replication in this step can be modified. For ENA extract plates from old specimens, we will usually do full length ITS and/or ITS2 (gITS7-ITS4) in triplicate for each specimen. If a specimen is very important, and didn't work with an initial attempt, we may lay out an entire row of ENA extractions from the backup tissue for the sample, and then try the 8 extracts in triplicate for PCR (24 total reaction attempts). The three key elements to play with are 1.) How many extracts to plate out from the original tissue. 2.) length of loci to attempt - for general collections over 10 years old, we likely only try ITS2. and 3.) how many replicates to attempt for that locus? We typically run museum specimens in triplicate, with the same index, and pool them. Amplification from Promega extracts: With this extraction protocol, diluting the template often washes out PCR inhibitors. Inversely, diluting the template can sometimes dilute out low quantities of DNA from not working during PCR at all. So for older herbarium specimens we take what we would call a "brute force" approach at PCR. For every specimen, we perform four PCR reactions before we look at the results. Two attempts with full length ITS and two attempts with different primers for ITS2. Within each of these, one attempt is at standard template dilution and the other attempt is with a 1:50 dilution of the template. So the permutations are full ITS no dilution, full ITS diluted, ITS2 no dilution, and ITS2 diluted. We perform no DNA quantifications on individual specimens nor run gels for any individual specimens before sequencing. PCR success is validated solely by whether the specimen was successfully sequenced - we do not run any gels to validate successful amplification. It takes up too much time and/or money for no benefit, because even if there is not a band, we would try sequencing for the sample anyway. Doing these four PCR reactions for each specimen up front has many advantages. The first is that you get most of the data for the first attempt, right up front, without the need to resort/reorder specimens and spreadsheets for a second PCR attempt. Secondarily, and perhaps most importantly, this process typically yields more than one sequence for the same specimen. This helps to self-validate the results you are getting, as the same sequence should result from different, independent PCR reactions, libraries, and primer combinations. Having this replicated data right up front significantly helps to aid confidence in the results during analysis.

steps.title: Decide Extraction Strategy
steps.instruction: Choose between the quick‑and‑dirty ENA extraction (for non‑collection‑quality DNA) or the clean Promega kit extraction (for collection‑quality DNA) based on future use and storage considerations.

steps.title: Prepare Sampling Spreadsheet
steps.instruction: Create a spreadsheet to track each specimen. For ENA, number wells 1‑1 to 1‑96 (plate 2 starts at 2‑1, etc.) and scan specimen barcodes into the corresponding well. For Promega, base the sheet on the layout of your cardboard freezer boxes or tube racks (e.g., 81‑tube box = sheet 1 with 81 rows).

steps.title: Collect Primary and Backup Tissue
steps.instruction: Using tweezers, remove the smallest possible piece of tissue from each specimen. Place the primary amount into the designated primary container and the backup amount into a secondary 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube.

substeps.instruction: For ENA: put primary tissue into a 96‑well PCR plate (or 8‑strip tubes with strip caps); put backup tissue into a 1.5 mL tube.
For Promega: put both primary and backup tissue into separate 1.5 mL tubes.
Use a piece roughly the size of a grain of rice or smaller so it settles at the tube bottom.

steps.title: Perform ENA Extraction
steps.instruction: If ENA was selected, follow the Extract‑N‑Amp Equivalent DNA Extraction steps:

substeps.instruction: Add 20 µL ENA solution and 50 µL extraction buffer to each well (total 70 µL) using a reservoir and multichannel pipette.
Add one 1 mm stainless‑steel ball bearing to each well (sterility not required as long as the bead has not been used for a prior extraction).
Place the plate on a BioSpec bead‑beater and beat for 5 minutes.
Heat the plate at 80 °C for 10 minutes.
Spin down the plate briefly; the lysate is now ready for PCR.

steps.title: Perform Promega Extraction
steps.instruction: If Promega was selected, follow the Modified Promega Wizard Extraction for Barcoding Macrofungi protocol as documented on the laboratory’s protocol page.

steps.title: Set Up Half‑Volume PCR
steps.instruction: Prepare a 12.5 µL “half” PCR reaction for each sample, adding 0.5 µL of the extraction template to each well and completing the remaining components according to the ONT DNA Barcoding Fungal Amplicons PCR mix.

steps.title: Pool and Prepare Libraries for ONT Sequencing
steps.instruction: Follow the ONT DNA Barcoding Fungal Amplicons with MinION & Flongle protocol for post‑PCR pooling, purification, dA‑tailing, adapter ligation, and library preparation.

substeps.instruction: For ENA extracts: aim for ~2 million reads per MinION flow cell for 960 specimens.
Allocate 60 PCR plates (10 plates × 3 replicates × 2 amplicon lengths) which generate two independent libraries (full‑length ITS undiluted and diluted).
For Promega extracts: also target ~2 million reads per flow cell but build four libraries (full‑length ITS undiluted, full‑length ITS diluted, and the two short‑amplicon libraries).
If fewer than 960 specimens are processed, combine permutations into a single library as appropriate.

steps.title: Run ONT Sequencing and Basecalling
steps.instruction: Load each prepared library onto a MinION or Flongle flow cell, run the sequencing according to the ONT protocol, and perform basecalling using the recommended ONT software.

steps.title: Analyze Data with Specimux and Speconsense
steps.instruction: Use Specimux and Speconsense pipelines to demultiplex permutational libraries, parse variants, and build consensus sequences for downstream analysis.
